In the browser the simulation runs in one module Web Worker that also runs the local server and owns the network connection; the page posts its newest input to the Worker once per drawn frame and the Worker sends the page one transferred block per tick, so nothing crosses per entity and the page never calls into Wasm.

The lobby gets a crate when ADR 0006 decides where it runs (OQ-0006-3: inside the supervisor's binary or as its own service); until then no lobby crate is created.

`room` and `client-endpoint` build for `wasm32-unknown-unknown` and natively, with no async runtime, no transport crate and no wasm-bindgen (the same two tools), and read no clock (part 7's clock ban);

`sim-worker` and `net` never import rendering or DOM packages; nothing imports `legacy/` or `spikes/`; every Rust dependency comes from crates.io, checked by cargo-deny's `sources` class at deny (proposed:
R5-GATE-F3 lists the class, r5 lines 954–960, but its options were not read; the security review's finding 10), so a git or other-registry dependency fails G5.

`sim` is built with one feature set on every target: it exposes no feature that changes maths, the maths-relevant features of the dependencies it shares with `server` are set once in `[workspace.dependencies]`, and the gate compares the resolved feature list of every `sim` dependency (`cargo tree -e features`) across every build that runs the sim (`server`, `devtools`, `navbake` and `sim-wasm`), each made by the exact command CI and the release use, since Cargo unifies features over everything one command builds (R5-LAYOUT-F4).
- Changed from R5-LAYOUT-REC2 (r5 lines 1170–1193): three crates are added and none removed.

`client-endpoint`, because ADR 0001's network marks run the client endpoint's Rust code natively and headless, and so do the soak and load layers (part 8), while R5-LAYOUT-REC2 names no crate for that code but the bindings crate: the headless clients would otherwise need a native build of a bindings crate or a second copy of the endpoint.
The code is the same; only its crate is new.
The first two answer questions the critic gave this record and the third follows from ADR 0001's headless tests; no research compared them with other placements.

All three are proposed (not researched): no research Options section offers a crate for the room logic, the client endpoint or the bake, and SLICE-ORDER condition 1 and R4-XT-OQ5 leave them to this record; whether plan rule 3 allows that is OQ-0002-8, for the Advisor at the stop.
The supervisor's crate (slice 3) is beyond R5's list too, but the research asks for it:
R6-HOST-REC2 puts a small supervisor on every VM (r6-infrastructure.md lines 645–647), which ADR 0006 part 5 adopts.

A trap carries no panic message, so the Wasm build's panic hook (ADR 0004 part 20, S20) writes the message and location into a fixed buffer in linear memory, and when the instance traps the Worker's host reads that buffer, through a fresh view of the memory (part 5), and attaches it to the trap's report.

The server is built for baseline x86-64, never with `+fma`, `-C target-cpu=native` or the `relaxed-simd` target feature: the gate reads the build flags of `sim`, `room`, `client-endpoint`, `sim-wasm` and `server` and fails if one appears (the rule is ADR 0004's, part 7; the check is this record's).

If wasm-opt is kept (R5-CI-OQ4), the check reads its command line too, because wasm-opt optimizes the shipped Wasm after rustc: it fails on binaryen's `--fast-math` (`-ffm`, "Optimize floats without handling corner cases of NaNs, rounding, and negative zero" in binaryen's own options, read by rust-reviewer at the step-10 review; not in the research) and on any feature flag beyond the target's defaults (R1-BND-F19's list, r1 lines 1019–1025), `relaxed-simd` above all.

It holds a header (tick, layout hash, counts per entity kind), aligned sections per entity kind (soldiers, vehicle parts, projectiles, structures, weapon pickups, which are sim entities under UPGRADE-SCOPE, ADR 0004 part 18), one section of owner-only data for the local player (own weapon state, money, upgrade tracks and offers: decision map I-21; the floor layer and enclosure area id the roof fade needs:

ADR 0004 part 14) and the event section (the events of ADR 0004 part 19: hits, deaths and kills, blasts, cosmetic shot events, purchases, uplink cache events, harvester deliveries and kills, structure kills and stage changes, tech tiers, upgrade picks and pickups, and the moments its moment phase emits;

The event section holds the events due at that block, each on the timeline of the entity it belongs to: the Worker releases a remote entity's spatial event (an action start, a death, a blast on the entity it hit) when its interpolation clock reaches the event's tick, and the local player's own, predicted and owner events at once; a local match does the same, since its client endpoint is the same code (the rule is ADR 0001 part 7's; r2-netcode.md, Recommendations, Brief question 1, R2-SYNC-REC6, line 2210: blasts "played on the timeline of the entity they hit").

The block writer serializes field by field (R1-DET-REC6's method for [the state hash](../research/GLOSSARY.md#state-hash), applied to the block), so struct padding never reaches the page and no `unsafe` is needed.

R1-RR-OQ6's decider, rust-reviewer, confirmed this at the step-10 review on three conditions: one layout table in Rust drives the writer, the generated offsets and the layout hash, so the three cannot drift; every integer is written at a fixed width (never `usize`) and little-endian (`to_le_bytes`); each section is aligned to its largest element type, so the page's typed-array views bind with no copy.

R1-RR-OQ6's two alternatives (a derive that rejects padding, or `unsafe` with a written invariant and a test) are weighed only if the writer's p99 in Wasm on the minimum laptop exceeds 5 % of the client's sim share at 30 Hz (0.05 × 13.33 = 0.67 ms; proposed by rust-reviewer: below that the writer cannot decide that mark).

- **The newest input, posted once per drawn frame,** from the page to the Worker (option C1, changed in its cadence): a sequence number, the move input, the held-button bitmask and press and release edge counters kept as running totals (their exact fields are ADR 0001's), plus the camera's cursor ray and the view time of the frame the page drew.

At each tick the Worker takes the newest post (the running totals mean a superseded post loses no press), casts its ray against the state it published for that view time and fills the tick's one network command, aim point included (ADR 0001 part 5; decision map I-19), so the aim needs no second message.
The Worker stamps the tick it applies the input to.

Why per frame: the page has no tick clock (its only tick signal is the block), so a post per block can leave a press waiting up to two tick periods less the block's delivery before a tick applies it (2 × 1000 / 30 = 66.67 ms at 30 Hz), against R1-BND-REC3 mark 2's one tick plus one frame (33.33 + 16.67 = 50.00 ms with a 60 Hz display; r1-simulation-core.md, Recommendations, unit boundary-worker, R1-BND-REC3, lines 2286–2296); a post per frame bounds the wait by one frame plus one tick plus the message's delivery, and the page's work stays one small message per frame.
Each tick the Worker's host makes one input call and one step call.

The input call carries the page's newest input; every datagram received since the last tick, each with the time it arrived (the host's `performance.now()` in that datagram's own message event, never the tick's time); the time the host sent the previous step's datagrams; and the host's current time, all as plain values, since Rust reads no clock of its own (part 7).

Without arrival times every clock and jitter sample of ADR 0001 parts 5 and 7 would carry up to one tick period of false jitter (0 to 1000 / 30 = 33.33 ms at 30 Hz); those samples use the stamps, and how a ping answered at the next tick reports its hold time is ADR 0001's (part 5).

The step leaves the outgoing datagrams and the block in linear memory and returns where they lie and when the next tick is due: in local play from the plain accumulator, online from the client endpoint's server-time estimate, since online the Worker's tick runs ahead of the server's by ADR 0001's rule for keeping commands just in time (OQ-0001-6).
The host sets its timer from that, never from a count of its own, and the catch-up it allows is counted per wake of the Worker, at most 7 ticks (ADR 0004 part 5, S18).
The host reads the step's output through a fresh view of the instance's `memory.buffer` after every call, never a cached one, since growth makes an old view stale (proposed:
R1-BND-REC2 names re-binding on growth as a cost of B4, r1 lines 2273–2274).

- **Generated types, from three sources, into one committed package** `packages/types`: wasm-bindgen's `.d.ts` and glue are build output (ignored); our own small generator writes the block's layout (offsets, strides, element types) and its layout hash from the layout table the writer uses (above), and the page checks the hash at startup (option D4); ts-rs writes the protocol and message types into `packages/types/src/generated/` on `cargo test`, through `TS_RS_EXPORT_DIR` in `.cargo/config.toml` (option D3); content's types land in the same package, from the source ADR 0005 picks (critic rank 31).

The generators' derives never reach a shipped build: ts-rs is a dev-dependency, and its derives sit behind `cfg_attr(test, …)` or, where one crate's types nest another's, behind a feature that only dev-dependency entries turn on ("Dev-dependencies do not activate features unless building a Cargo target that needs them":

R5-LAYOUT-F4, r5 lines 83–91), so the builds part 3 compares and G7 measures are the shipped ones (proposed by rust-reviewer at the step-10 review); content's schema generator follows the same rule (ADR 0005, CD-3).

- Why: the tick leaves the render thread; one bounded copy per tick needs neither isolation nor nightly Rust; one small message per frame is constant work and keeps a press within one tick plus one frame of the tick that applies it; the block's layout is the only thing tsify and ts-rs cannot type.

The Worker's host (TypeScript) receives the page's inputs, paces the tick (ADR 0004 part 5), steps the instance or instances, and posts each block; the inputs it forwards pass through it, outside the Wasm instance, which is what OQ-0004-7's recovery options need to know.

In a local match one Worker step runs in this order: the client endpoint builds tick T's command from the newest input (its aim cast included) and predicts T with the sim's prediction step (ADR 0004 part 3); the command reaches the local server through the loopback; the local server runs tick T with the authority step and every slot's command (the bots' through the same input path) and encodes T's snapshot and events; the client endpoint decodes them, reconciles and writes the block.

So the command for tick T reaches the local server before it runs T, and a local input never waits an extra step (the spike's item 3); with two instances (OQ-0002-3 (b)) the host makes its calls in the same order.

The Worker as a whole has no budget in the research: the client's sim share covers the sim step only (GLOSSARY, the client's sim share, lines 214–218), so the boundary spike reports the Worker's busy time per tick in both modes and its JS heap and Wasm memory over a match (item 6), and this record sets any limit on them from those numbers.
So that a strict content security policy stays possible, the build is CSP-ready, as ADR 0006's interim position for B3 asks (proposed, not researched; the security review's finding 11):

ESLint's core `no-eval` and `no-new-func` are on at error (their pages were not read), the built HTML holds no inline script or style, and the Worker and the Wasm load as files, never from `blob:` or `data:` URLs (checked in G8).

`Instant::now`, `SystemTime::now`, the `algebraic_*` methods and every std `f32` and `f64` method outside ADR 0004 part 7's allow-list and the exact methods the rules themselves use, such as `is_finite`, `is_nan`, `to_bits` and `total_cmp`), at deny, with `iter_over_hash_type` as a backstop.

The float ban is written as the allow-list's complement because ADR 0004 part 7 is an allow-list (R1-DET-REC2, r1-simulation-core.md, Recommendations, lines 2146–2150): it names every other method on the pinned std's `f32` and `f64` pages and is read again at every Rust bump (part 2).
So it catches more than the transcendental functions:

`powi`, `hypot` and `cbrt` carry std's note that their precision varies by platform and Rust version (R1-DET-F9, r1 lines 648–654, inferred there; rust-reviewer confirmed the note for these three and for `to_degrees` and `to_radians` on std 1.99.1's `f32` page at the step-10 review), and `min`, `max` and `clamp` may return either zero for equal signed zeros, while `clamp` panics on bad bounds (R1-DET-F14, r1 lines 679–683).
The sim uses three helpers of its own for those three, written as plain comparisons, with one defined result for equal zeros and no panic (proposed).
The only escape from the hash-map ban is a reviewed `#[allow]` with a written reason for a map that is only looked up and lies outside the serialized sim state (resolution 29).

The clock ban (`Instant::now` and `SystemTime::now` in `disallowed-methods`, at deny) also lives in the `clippy.toml` of `room`, `protocol`, `client-endpoint` and `sim-wasm`, for two reasons: these crates run in the Worker, where std's clock calls panic on `wasm32-unknown-unknown` (std's own source, read by rust-reviewer at the step-10 review; not in the research) and the target's `-Cpanic=abort` makes that panic a trap (R1-BND-F19, r1 lines 1019–1025), which native tests never see; and a timer counted in ticks replays exactly, as SLICE-ORDER's replayable matches need.
So room timers count ticks, with their lengths in data; the client endpoint takes time only as the values the host passes in (part 5); only `server` reads `Instant`.
Which timers are tick-counted in `room` and which run on wall time in `server` (such as the join deadline and the per-connection rate limits) is ADR 0001's (parts 5 and 11).
In `protocol`'s decoders and `content`'s loader, `unwrap_used`, `expect_used` and `indexing_slicing` are at deny, allowed in tests.

In the sim they are at deny in the module that applies commands, where values a client or content can set enter (an offer and its choice, a purchase's unit id, a team or slot setting), so those values reach the rest of the sim only through checked lookups (ADR 0004 part 20;

PM-0004-60 fuzzes it); elsewhere the sim's indices come from its own pools. rustfmt runs with stable options only (`edition` and `style_edition` 2024, `newline_style = "Unix"`), in check mode in the gate.

Playwright opens a replay page that runs the `sim-wasm` Worker in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit and returns the hash stream; every Wasm run uses the exact file G6 ships and G7 measures (after wasm-bindgen and wasm-opt, checked by its hash); a comparer reports the first mismatching tick and a field-level diff.

- **Soak and load:** bots as headless Rust clients that speak the real protocol (on `client-endpoint`, part 3); one nightly run per mode of [the test-mode list](../research/GLOSSARY.md#the-test-mode-list) over L1 at P2, 30 minutes each, and one L2 run with 4 real browser clients among the bots.

On CI's shared runners a run is judged only by what needs no particular machine: desyncs, panics and hangs, the resident-memory slope, queue lengths, bytes per client per second, plus legacy TL13's match metrics;

[server tick time](../research/GLOSSARY.md#server-tick-time) p50, [p99](../research/GLOSSARY.md#time-statistics) and max is reported there, and judged against [the server tick budget](../research/GLOSSARY.md#the-server-tick-budget) (ADR 0001's) only from a run on one vCPU of the reference server (PM-0002-72), since timings on shared runners are not hardware results.
Before each playtest one 3-hour soak runs on the reference server, so its tick times count (its VM: the bench's path below).

`failOnFlakyTests` and `forbidOnly` on in CI); one committed fixed `PROPTEST_RNG_SEED` in the gate, fresh seeds nightly with every failure committed to `proptest-regressions` with its fix; simulated time only in sim and network tests; browser tests wait on state through a test-hook API and drive page time with Playwright's clock; no shared global state in Rust tests; every failure keeps its seed, recording and trace as CI artefacts, for the retention ADR 0006 sets for failure artefacts (part 3;
R5 leaves it to infra-engineer, r5 line 2083; until it is set, the 7 days of build artifacts), and gets an issue that carries the seed, so the failure still replays after its artefacts expire.

The bench needs the reference server from slice 1, before ADR 0006's fleet exists, and CI holds no token for it (timings on shared runners are not hardware results): it runs on a CCX23 created per bench session in the spikes' own Hetzner project and deleted after it, ADR 0006 part 8's cost line (proposed there:

20 bench hours a month, 20 × 0.1386 = 2.77 EUR, R6-HOST-F15, r6 lines 150–158), and who creates and deletes it without a session reading a secret is OQ-0006-17; the 3-hour soak before each playtest uses the same path.

By the research's own findings every CI browser probably gets no WebGPU adapter and falls back to WebGL 2:

Chrome on Linux offers WebGPU only on Intel Gen12+ GPUs (R3-WGPU-F17, r3-rendering.md lines 159–162), Firefox not on Linux (R3-WGPU-F18, r3 lines 164–169), any browser with no adapter falls back (R3-GL2-F12, r3 lines 279–283), and headless Chrome renders on "SwiftShader Device (Subzero)" (R3-MEASURE-F8, r3 lines 648–653);
Playwright's WebKit on Linux, and whether headless Firefox and WebKit get WebGL 2 at all, were not researched.

Then the default run repeats the `forceWebGL` run and CI never runs the WebGPU backend, so a shader that fails to build for WebGPU, a WebGPU validation error or a pipeline made mid-match only on WebGPU would pass CI.
The foundation therefore records, per CI engine, the backend it gets (or none).
If none gets WebGPU, the boundary spike tries a Chromium job with SwiftShader's WebGPU adapter turned on by flags, for counts and errors only (not researched;

R3-MEASURE-F8 names GPU flags only for hardware runs); until a CI route works, every change-set that touches the render path carries a WebGPU smoke run (console errors, ADR 0003's counts, the backend string) on a reference machine of ADR 0003 as stated evidence.

The job that uploads debug files for Sentry (R6-OBS-REC3) runs only on builds that are deployed, in its own GitHub environment that holds the Sentry token, with no checkout of pull-request code, shaped like the deploy job it follows and under that job's guard (part 10:
`production`'s `main`-only branch rule, or `preview`'s required reviewer for a preview); its token scope is ADR 0006's (part 13, item B9).

**The preview build.** Shape P1: the ordinary `pull_request` workflow builds with no secret and uploads `dist` as an artifact (kept 7 days, the retention ADR 0006 sets); a separate deploy job (`needs: build`) runs in a GitHub environment named `preview`, holds the client-host token for previews, never checks out or runs pull-request code, runs only for pull requests from this repository, has the permissions `contents: read`, `actions: read`, `deployments: write` and `pull-requests: write`, turns automatic package caching off, sets the environment's URL to the preview link and posts or updates one comment with it.

One gap remains: a `pull_request` run takes its workflow from the pull request's own merge commit (the contrast R5-PREV-F2 draws with `pull_request_target`, r5 lines 770–774; the security review's reading at step 10), so any branch of this repository, which agent sessions push, can rewrite the deploy job and use its token.

That token is account-scoped (R5-PREV-F10, r5 lines 823–830), and the deploy command's `branch` option that finding quotes lets one deploy name any branch, so the token can probably reach production too (an inference; the client host's production rules were not read).
Until the security baseline rules on CI tokens, ADR 0006's interim position for B9 (part 13) closes the gap:
`preview` has a required reviewer, so each preview deploy waits for Mustafa's approval ("a job cannot access environment secrets until one of the required reviewers approves it":

R5-PREV-F6, r5 lines 796–804), unless OQ-0006-13 puts production where the preview token cannot reach it; whether a session, which posts as Mustafa's account (CLAUDE.md), could approve a pending deploy was not read and is part of OQ-0006-13.

**Production** is deployed only by its own job, on pushes to `main`, from the artifact `main`'s CI built and tested, in its own environment `production` that holds its own client-host token behind a deployment-branch rule admitting `main` alone ("Deployment branches and tags are available for all public repositories":
R5-PREV-F6; the repository is public: r5 lines 752–754); when a release goes out beside running rooms is ADR 0006's.

CI's native job builds the room binary like any other artifact; a delivery job shaped like the deploy job, in its own environment with the same required reviewer as `preview` (B9's interim position), hands that binary to the staging game server's supervisor and receives the current and the next certificate hash; the preview deploy job writes both into the preview's own files, which the page fetches from its own HTTPS origin (ADR 0001, part 10).

One hash would go stale: a self-signed certificate lives at most 14 days (R2-TRN-REC5, r2-netcode.md, Recommendations, Brief question 4, lines 2700–2703), and R2-TRN-REC5 mark 2 asks that new connections succeed with the new hash within one reload (r2 lines 2720–2721), which a static file cannot give.

So on the staging VM the supervisor, not each room process, holds the certificate, rotates it every 7 days and makes the next one a full period ahead, and a preview older than one rotation is redeployed (ADR 0006, part 4; proposed, not researched).

If OQ-0006-5 instead gives the staging server, on both transports, the browser-trusted certificate its `wss` endpoint needs anyway (the kind R2-TRN-REC5 gives production, r2 line 2704), a multiplayer preview pins no hash and the delivery job hands over only the binary.
The delivery token's scope, and whether pull-request-built native code may run on the staging game server, wait for the security baseline (ADR 0006, part 13, item B9).

- **A Worker, one block out per tick and the newest input in per frame** wins over the main thread and over shared memory because the tick leaves the render thread, the work per tick is constant in N, and nothing needs cross-origin isolation, nightly Rust or a fixed memory maximum.

- **Three crates beyond R5's list** (`room`, `client-endpoint`, `navbake`) cost three more dependency checks; without them the local server cannot run in the Worker, the headless clients of ADR 0001's network marks and of the soaks would need a native build of the bindings crate or a second copy of the client endpoint, and the bake's generator would risk shipping in the player's Wasm.
